title: Doubt vs fear: determinate assent may remain with fear that things could be otherwise
source_text: VIII. Verum licet omnis certitudo dubitationem excludat, juxta mentem Doctorum Ecclesiae Romanae, non excludit tamen omnem formidinem. Nam secundum eorum doctrinam, aliud est dubitare, aliud vero formidare. Qui dubitat, ut jam dixi, judicium plane suspendit, & inter utramque partem contradictionis quasi neuter & medius haeret. Qui vero circa unam contradictionis partem judicium definitum & determinatum format, & statuit rem ita se habere; & simul tamen judicat fieri posse ut res aliter se habeat, ille non dubitare quidem, sed formidare proprie dicitur. Sic, exempli gratia, qui accepta syngrapha alicujus hominis ipsi noti nomen praeferente, postquam scripturae modum & literarum ductus atque figuras diligenter inspexit, determinate & absque haesitatione judicat illam esse illius hominis, de eo certus dici potest: & tamen simul judicat non impossibile esse quin daemon, aut aliquis exercitatus & insignis impostor tale quidpiam effingeret. Ac proinde juxta Scholae Romanae stylum, in eo quidem homine circa rem propositam non erit dubitatio, sed tamen circa istud non carebit omni formidine.
pass_a_gloss: Yet although every certainty excludes doubt according to the mind of the Roman doctors, it does not therefore exclude every fear. For according to their doctrine, to doubt is one thing, to fear another. He who doubts, as I have already said, altogether suspends judgment and hangs as it were neutral and middle between both sides of the contradiction. But he who forms a definite and determinate judgment about one side of the contradiction and decides that the matter is so, and yet at the same time judges that it can happen that the matter is otherwise—he is said not indeed to doubt, but properly to fear. Thus, for example, one who, having received a note bearing the name of a man known to him, after diligently inspecting the manner of writing and the strokes and shapes of the letters, determinately and without hesitation judges it to be that man’s, can be called certain of it; and yet at the same time judges it not impossible that a demon, or some practiced and notable impostor, might forge such a thing. And therefore, in the Roman School’s style, in that person concerning the matter proposed there will not be doubt, yet concerning that matter he will not be free of all fear.
pass_b_english: Romans separate doubt (suspended judgment) from fear (firm assent that still allows the opposite).
Recognizing a familiar signature can be certain yet still admit fear of clever forgery.
